column3: Normalise the objectives, minimise w₁f₁+w₂f₂ with a scalar solver for 21 weights between 0 and 1, keep the non-dominated results.
column4: • Extremely simple: one scalarisation + any single-objective solver.; • Accurate on convex fronts: IGD 0.020 on P1 with 21 distinct points †.; • Each solution is Pareto-optimal for w>0 (guaranteed by theory).; • Scales to many objectives (longer weight vector) and the weights are easy for a decision maker to read.; • Cheap per point (all 21 solves took 0.4s on P1 †).
column5: • Cannot reach dented regions: only 2 distinct points on non-convex P3 and 0 with 0.25<f₁<0.75 †.; • Equal weight steps do not give equal spacing: on P4 only 17 of 21 weights gave distinct points (Spacing 0.063) †.; • Each point needs a whole solver run (172,116 evaluations for 21 points on P1 †) – far more than the 10,000 budget of the population methods.; • Sensitive to objective scaling (needs normalisation) and to weights.; • No handling of integer/discrete fronts unless the solver supports them.
column6: Convex continuous problems with a fast scalar solver (P1, P4 portfolio).
column7: Non-convex or discontinuous fronts (P3), or when evenly spread points are needed.

column3: Minimise one objective while the others are bounded by ε (swept from ideal to nadir in 21 steps); each solve gives one Pareto point.
column4: • Reaches non-convex fronts: 21 points, IGD 0.025 on P3 (weighted sum got 2) †.; • Handles constraints naturally (P5: HV 0.819, IGD 0.021) †.; • Spread is controlled directly by the ε grid.; • Works for convex, concave and mixed fronts; solutions are Pareto-optimal when the ε-constraint is active.; • Uses a plain single-objective constrained solver.
column5: • ε grid is uniform in one objective, so points are uneven in objective space (Spacing 0.129 on P2) †.; • One constrained solve per point: 217,200 evaluations on P3 †.; • Needs ideal and nadir values to choose ε; an ε that is too tight is infeasible.; • Grid size grows as 21^(M−1) for M objectives – impractical beyond 3 objectives.; • May return weakly Pareto-optimal points if the bound is inactive.
column6: 2–3 objectives, non-convex or constrained, with a reliable scalar solver (P3, P5).
column7: Many objectives (M ≥ 5) or when the nadir point is unknown.

column3: From a feasible starting design x⁰ maximise Σwᵢ(fᵢ(x⁰)−fᵢ(x)) subject to f(x) ≤ f(x⁰); the result is a Pareto point that dominates x⁰.
column4: • Guarantees an improvement: the output dominates the start (checked in the unit test).; • Works on linear P7 and convex P1 (HV 0.606 and 0.970) †.; • Needs no ideal/nadir point and no weights to be tuned – the start design plays the role of a reference point.; • Natural tool to improve an existing design.; • Cheap: 98,352 evaluations for 12 starts †.
column5: • Coverage depends on the starts: 11 distinct points from 12 starts on P1, Spacing 0.130 (uneven) †.; • IGD 0.073 on P1 is worse than weighted sum's 0.020 † because starts cluster.; • Needs a feasible start (P7 required rejection sampling).; • One constrained nonlinear solve per start; the feasible set f(x) ≤ f(x⁰) can be thin and hard for the solver.; • No control of the spread of the final set.
column6: Improving a given feasible design (what-can-I-gain-for-free questions).
column7: When a uniform picture of the whole front is required.

column3: Minimise the weighted distance to the ideal point, (Σ(wᵢfᵢ)^p)^(1/p) for p = 1, 2 or max(wᵢfᵢ) for p = ∞ (Tchebycheff), over a weight sweep.
column4: • p = ∞ recovers the whole non-convex front: 21 points, IGD 0.018 on P3 †.; • p = 1 reproduces weighted sum, so one family covers a range of behaviours (2 points on P3 for p=1, 13 for p=2) †.; • Ideal point gives an intuitive 'closest to perfect' reading of preferences.; • Normalised version is scale-free.; • Good spacing on P1 for p=1 (Spacing 0.008) †.
column5: • p = 2 only partly reaches non-convex parts (13 points, IGD 0.100 on P3) †.; • Needs the ideal point first, i.e. M extra single-objective solves.; • Spacing depends on p: 0.008 for p=1 vs 0.033 for p=∞ on P1 †.; • p = ∞ is non-smooth and can return weakly Pareto-optimal points.; • Whole sweep costs 218,080 evaluations on P3 †.
column6: Non-convex fronts with a known ideal point when a scalar solver is available (p = ∞).
column7: p = 1 on non-convex fronts; very high-dimensional objective spaces (sweep size).

column3: The decision maker supplies a utility U(f); one scalar optimisation maximises U and returns the single preferred solution.
column4: • Returns the answer directly, no post-selection: one solve (8,376 evaluations on P14) †.; • Handles any shape of preference: on P14 it found exactly (1.800 kg, 12.00 h) †.; • Works with constraints and any number of objectives.; • Changing the utility parameter moves the solution along the front (sensitivity study in Task C).
column5: • Needs the DM to know the utility in advance (hard in practice).; • A badly chosen utility returns a dominated design: the target-distance utility on P14 chose screen 14.5″ although every Pareto point has x₁ = 13″ †.; • One solution only – no picture of the trade-off.; • Non-monotone utilities create local optima and need global solvers.; • For P4 three investor profiles needed three separate solves (8,376 evaluations) †.
column6: A priori preference is known (target design such as P14).
column7: Exploratory design when the DM wants to see the front.

column3: Targets for each objective, deviation variables d⁺, d⁻, minimise the weighted undesirable deviations subject to the constraints.
column4: • Works directly in natural units and reports how much each goal is missed: P11 shortfall of the units goal = 100 †.; • Exact on linear problems: P11 solution [300.0, 200.0] = the analytic vertex (300, 200) †.; • Goals that are over-ambitious still give a best compromise instead of 'infeasible'.; • Weights express priorities; one solve gives one answer.
column5: • Result depends on weights and goal values: on P7 weights (10,1) give outputs [40.0, 48.0] but (1,10) give [38.7, 50.0] †.; • Unit weights mix incommensurable units: on P7 unit weights give outputs [38.7, 50.0] but weights normalised by the goals give [38.7, 50.0] †.; • If the goals are pessimistic the solution may be dominated (goal attained, but better designs exist).; • Gives one point, not a front.; • Goal values require prior knowledge of what is attainable.
column6: Planning problems with explicit targets (production, budgets – P11, P7).
column7: When goals are unknown or when a Pareto front is the deliverable.

column3: Optimise objectives strictly in priority order; each later problem keeps the earlier optimum within a tolerance.
column4: • Needs no weights; breaks ties exactly: on P11 profit 2400 is kept and units rise to 500 at (300,200) †.; • Exact priority: P7 agriculture-first returns x₁ = 70.0, the maximum possible 70 †.; • Matches how some organisations really decide (safety first, cost second).; • Handles constraints through the underlying solver.
column5: • Lower priorities are ignored unless there are ties: on P7 agriculture-first gives [56.0, 24.0], industry-first [8.0, 96.0] (two extreme points) †.; • The tolerance (here 0.5 %) is a hidden sensitive parameter: too small gives a thin feasible slab the solver cannot find, too large lets priority 1 leak.; • Gives only one point, an extreme with respect to priority 1.; • An exact tie is needed for later objectives to matter (P11: the profit ridge) †.; • Priority order must be known.
column7: Objectives of comparable importance – you get extreme solutions.

column3: Vector-normalise and weight the decision matrix, compute distance to the ideal and anti-ideal alternatives, rank by closeness C = d⁻/(d⁺+d⁻).
column4: • Closed-form, no optimisation, runs in microseconds.; • Ranks any finite set, e.g. P12 (S3 > S1 > S5 > S2 > S4, C = [0.621, 0.476, 0.63, 0.37, 0.597]) †.; • All 5 suppliers of P12 are Pareto-optimal, yet TOPSIS still gives a complete order (S3 first) †.; • Easy to explain: closest to ideal and farthest from worst.; • Works on a front produced by NSGA-II (Task D).
column5: • Fully compensatory: a supplier with reliability 40 % still ranks #1 when it is excellent elsewhere †.; • Ranking flips under a 0.1 weight shift in 4 of 4 tested shifts on P12 †.; • Needs weights from the decision maker and a normalisation choice that changes the answer.; • Not an optimiser: it cannot create alternatives, only rank given ones.; • Rank reversal when alternatives are added.
column6: Selecting from a finite list or from a Pareto front with agreed weights.
column7: When one criterion must never be very bad (use VIKOR with v small).

column3: Group utility S, individual regret R, Q = vS+(1−v)R; rank by smallest Q and test acceptable-advantage (C1) and stability (C2).
column4: • Parameter v trades average performance against worst-criterion regret: with v = 0 supplier S6 (40 % reliability) is ranked #3 but with v = 0.5 it is #1 †.; • C1/C2 tell you whether a single winner is justified (P12: C1=False, C2=True) †.; • Returns a compromise set rather than forcing one winner.; • Closed form, fast.; • Less compensatory than TOPSIS.
column5: • Ranking flips under a 0.1 weight shift in 2 of 4 tested shifts (v = .5) †.; • Winner changes with v on P12: ['S1', 'S1', 'S1'] for v = .25/.5/.75 †.; • Needs weights and v from the DM.; • When C1 fails the answer is a set of alternatives, not one.; • Not an optimiser; only ranks given alternatives.
column6: Group decisions where a very bad criterion is unacceptable.
column7: Large alternative sets where C1's 1/(J−1) threshold is meaningless.
